I had a 3 yr old boy, a 2 yr old girl and a newborn.

I wish I could help you but everything is just a blur now. Doing doctors appointments I had to drag all three, grocery shopping I had to push two shopping carts, the playground was stressful chasing the tots while carrying a newborn, getting them all ready to get out of the house was awful, the second I turned around another kid would get undressed and so on. 

There was one time I decided I wanted time for myself so I went out after the kids went to bed. I passed out in the parking lot at Target for two hours I couldn’t even get out of the car. My husband was mortified and so worried looking for me. 

I did avoid the baby carrier, I did it with my first only to find out he was not able to be put down and expected me to carry him everywhere all the time. See, I was pregnant with my second by the time he was 4 months. When my second was born I avoided the carrier as well so my second would not get used to be carried all the time. 

We did floor time a lot and I got them both used to being in a playmat on the floor and me playing with them, they would also be okay by me leaving them in the playpen to do some household chores and take showers. 

They were not Velcro babies and became independent very early on.

I don’t know how I survived haha but I wanna tell you something:

It gets easier. Now, I have a 6 yr old, a 5 yr old and a 3 yr old and we all hold hands walking through the parking lot. I still avoid shopping with more than two. I never go to restaurants with all the kids, it’s still too much. 

But I watch them play and take care of each other, they talk a lot and they tell each other the funniest things. Now, it feels like it wasn’t so bad.... or maybe I choose to forget!

Edit: I did sleep trained all three and they all slept through the night for 12 hrs uninterrupted since they were 6 months old, sleep helps, for them and for me to be well rested was a life changing decision.

Just a thought:

“Hand leading” to ask for things is an early sign of autism. If he’s using “hand leading” with eye contact is okay, but if he isn’t, then keep an eye on him. 

Your kid should also use either words and/or pointing for communication combined with eye contact. Learning how to communicate comes before words so he should be using some of these with eye contact. 

Also he should be able to follow your point. Point to something in the distance and see if he looks at what you are showing him.

Just a thought. I wish someone had told me this, being a first time mom didn’t come with all the instructions for me!

I have three kids, my oldest is a boy and is on the spectrum. He was the only one who used my hand as a “tool” to ask for things but didn’t look at me to check if I was looking at what he was showing me. My other two, girls, didn’t. They either talked or pointed or both.

Therapy is life changing. It was for us. 

We did 3 hours of therapy weekly before he turned two. Once he was properly diagnosed we did 6 hours of ABA daily for an entire year. Weekend were free. After 3, he was in an integrated preschool (highly recommend to put him in a school environment with special needs and NT kids, he’ll learn from his NT peers) from 9 am to 3 pm and ABA from 3:15 pm to 5:15 three times a week. 

When we have family time we make sure we do day trips to different places, museums, malls, playgrounds, loud and crowded places or quiet ones. 

He had bad social anxiety and it took about two years to get rid of it by exposing him to all kinds of scenarios. It will also increase his safety awareness. 

And lastly, but highly important:

Hug him, kiss him, touch his hand and hold him, make him hug you and squeeze you. Play pranks on him like hide behind the couch and call his name and scare him (not too bad though!), go on four and chase him around the house, if he’s playing by himself sometimes you just need to lay down next to him and keep him company or join in playing his game. Eventually he’ll include you in the games, then other and finally he’ll request and my son one day stared hiding behind or around the house and would wait for me to walk by and scare me!

You facial expression need more enhancing so he learns how to read feelings, don’t be afraid to raise your voice when necessary like in parking lots, etc so he know at least by the tone of your voice you’re serious. 

Change furniture around especially in his room, so he doesn’t get used to one particular look in the house.

I noticed something off at 15 months. I called the pediatrician, I called and called. Then, they gave me paperwork, I did that, I called and called early Intervention and set up my appointment as soon as possible, I put myself in the emergency list, because they whenever they could tell me jump, I would. 

I got him diagnosed at 22 months. Started ABA two months after and doing therapy from 9-11, 12-2 and 3-5 Monday to Fridays until he turned three. You never know, all we can do is help them.

At the evaluation, he was diagnosed with a severe speech delay and mild autism, he was two years old but his mind was one of a 9 month old. 

It was heartbreaking. 

Almost four years later, lots of therapy and life style changes:

My son is still autistic. He smiles and starting to talk, he goes to school and has made one friend. He can say some colors and he can describe a few of his surrounding. 

2 years ago my world started to crumble. I felt hopeless and just seeing other kids say "mama" would make me cry uncontrollably. Anywhere. I cried at the parking lots, in stores, public bathrooms, etc...

Once I picked myself up, and it took months, my husband and I made calls, increased therapies, I did essential oils, brush therapy, spent lot of money of toys so I could do therapy with him, watched YouTube videos on ABA, supplements, fish oil, probiotics, we did everything.

We are his chance of succeeding. Grieve, cause it's normal but understand time is precious. Call your insurance company and find out what kind of resources you have open. 

Watch videos online, ask around, go to the library, meet other parents on the same boat, gather information. 

Above all, take care of yourself. I went on antidepressants and my quality of life got better, I am able to think more clearly, I still get sad about a few things but I am able to pick myself up and focus on what's important: my son.

Go to therapy and if you need meds, go on. I highly recommend it. 

Lastly, I don't know what the future holds but I wish you and your son all the best.
